utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Brdjanin, can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, and I can hear you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you repeat that? Because this was not on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can hear and understand the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. General Talic, can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED TALIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear and understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. May it please Your Honours, my name is Cayley. I appear on behalf of the Prosecutor with my colleague Ms. Korner, case manager Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, John Ackerman. I appear on behalf of Mr. Brdjanin along with Tania Radosavljevic, Milka Maglov, and Milos Peric. I want to apologise to the Chamber for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- delaying you this morning. It was just a big mix-up and I'm sorry about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It could happen to anyone. And for General Talic?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic, attorney at the Paris bar, replacing Mr. de Roux and Mr. Pitron, and I'm assisted by Mr. Fabien Masson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, while we are at this particular stage of the proceedings, may I have an explanation why Mr. Pitron and Mr. de Roux haven't honoured us with their presence for the last three days? As I understand, they are the Defence counsel for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, they are the Defence counsel for General Talic, and I think that they were prevented from coming. They have good reasons for not coming, but I'm afraid I don't know anything more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am not disputing the justification or the reasons that might be maybe keeping them from being present here. This raises a matter which I think I am duty-bound in open court to refer to your client, General Talic, who has his procedural and substantive rights, and it is my duty here as Presiding Judge, and also the duty of the other two Judges accompanying me in this trial, to ensure that these procedural and substantive rights of your client are observed and that he is happy with the situation, because obviously you will understand, Ms. Fauveau, that I would not definitely leave the door open for subsequent aggravations as has happened in other cases before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand fully the situation and your position, but perhaps General Talic could tell us more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. General Talic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED TALIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you understand the import of what I have just been discussing with attorney Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED TALIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, Your Honour. I, too, do not know the reason for their absence, but for the present, I do not mind being represented by Madam Natasha.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I would suppose, Ms. Fauveau, that this, obviously, you must not take it as a reflection in your regard. It is not meant to be like that and that's why I have been extremely careful. The position is that your client is definitely entitled to be represented as was properly allocated to him, with the Defence counsel that were appointed to represent him. He's definitely very ably represented by you, and you have shown that throughout these last two or three days, but I don't think the situation can be protracted or perpetuated and expect the Trial Chamber to remain silent about it. So perhaps you could pass on this message to Mr. de Roux and Pitron, especially now that I have heard General Talic confirm that he himself has not been informed of the reason underlying their absence from this courtroom. Is there any comments that you would like to make from the Prosecution side on this particular issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We understand, Your Honour. Your Honour, we noticed the same absence, and we had actually remarked on it. Our concern is only this: Our view is that Ms. Fauveau has been doing an excellent job so far, but nonetheless, it is Mr. de Roux and Mr. Pitron who are counsel on the record. We would not wish there to be any grounds for an appeal on the basis that General Talic was not represented by counsel of his choice. That's -- I think that's all that we wish to say. We understand that General Talic, not surprisingly, is happy with representation by Ms. Fauveau, but nonetheless, my understanding is that counsel on the record can only be absent if the client consents in full knowledge of the reasons why they are absent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why -- Yes. General Talic, I put the same -- I repeat the same question to you again. You have just heard what Ms. Korner from the Prosecution has stated, which is more -- not more or less, it is the precise description of what the legal position obtaining is. What I want from you is a clear yes/no indication as to whether you are prepared to continue with the hearing of this trial today now that these two lawyers have been absent for two subsequent days - and this is the third day in which none of them have shown up - whether you are prepared to go ahead or whether you would prefer to invoke your rights and have them present, particularly since you have not been told, informed, of the reasons for their absence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED TALIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am ready to continue the proceedings for today and tomorrow, and not longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Fauveau, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, could I make a suggestion that perhaps this question can be clarified next Monday, because Mr. de Roux will be present and I think he's more qualified to discuss the matter than I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But even as a matter of courtesy. I have worked as a Judge for the past 25 years, and when counsel is not able to show up, usually the Court is informed. I mean, over here, at least from what I have gathered the last week and a half, if from the Prosecution, for example, Ms. Korner considers -- thinks that her presence is not needed at any given moment because Mr. Cayley will be dealing with a particular witness, even though it's almost superficial, an explanation is forthcoming, and the Tribunal -- the Trial Chamber is informed. And I have closed my eyes temporarily for the first day because I thought that anything could have happened, and I didn't want to raise the issue. The second day, I started getting worried. Now it's the third day, and we -- I will not allow the situation to go on like this. And also -- I mean, I am going to make myself very clear. I will not -- I will also not allow the situation to become one which will serve as a pretext for General Talic or for Mr. Brdjanin -- so far I have no reason to complain -- to direct any complaints for the Defence team of Mr. Brdjanin -- as a pretext for a particular sitting or hearing or sitting not to take place, because then obviously -- you know as much as I do what the Rules provide, and we will apply them, no question about it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I quite understand your position, and I appreciate your request, but as my client is ready to continue for another two days with me, I would suggest that the matter be clarified with the lead counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. General Talic, one last question: You do not wish, I suppose now that you are happy with the situation, at least until tomorrow, to raise any complaints as far as yesterday and the day before are concerned, do you? You are happy with what happened yesterday and the day before, in other words, that the proceedings went on irrespective of the fact that the two counsel allocated to you were not present?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED TALIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not wish to make any objections regarding the proceedings so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, General Talic. You may sit down. Yes. I understand the awkwardness of the situation in which you find yourself, Ms. Fauveau. I appreciate the co-operation that you have shown during these two -- the past two days with the Trial Chamber and the co-operation which has actually helped us finish with the -- with what we had to do almost a day earlier in advance. And I thank you for that. So I would suggest that we now call in Dr. Donia for cross-examination by Mr. Ackerman -- accident-prone Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you've also failed to note the last few days that I'm older than you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sometimes I feel the weight of my age, too, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Donia, you are going to be cross-examined today by Mr. Ackerman, who represents Mr. Brdjanin here. Has the witness made the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How are you today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Ready to go home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ready to go to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: To go to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. When you -- I think on the first day of your testimony you interrupted the process to tell the Court that you had something you wished to disclose to the Court. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I have to make the same kind of a disclosure to you. I have a brother who is a professor at Ohio State University, Lima, and that gave me the opportunity to inquire of you. And I must say the report that came back was quite favourable, that you distinguished yourself by your presence there. So it would be fair that I tell you what I learned about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. The first thing I need you to know about the questions that I'll be asking you is that I have tried very hard to organise what I'm going to do today in such a way that we can get through rather quickly, because I understand that you are anxious to leave here on Saturday, and because of that, it's going to be a little bit disjointed but I think probably not too much so. Let me begin with just a kind of general discussion of what history is and what historians do. Would you agree with me that history is a study of the activities of a certain group of people in a certain time and place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At least that's close to how an historian might define what that is; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is a -- one of the things that historians do is they do research and write the results of that research either in journals or books or papers or whatever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And there is a method that has developed over the years to kind of guide the process of historical research; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Primarily what you're doing is when you are trying to research a particular group of people at a certain time and place is that you look for sources of reliable information regarding what those people were doing at that time and place that you happened to be interested in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And I think I would add sources about that group's relationships with their environment, with other groups, and their broader situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And among the kinds of sources that you consult in that process, I think the method that we are talking about has divided them into basically two categories. There are primary sources and there are secondary sources; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is not always easy to draw a line between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Chamber what the difference is between a primary source and a secondary source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A primary source is any document or piece of evidence which comes from an identifiable creator and is generally not disseminated widely unless it is by publication in some collection or other -- other medium of dissemination. I think the most important factor would be the fact that its creator is knowable and identifiable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just as an example, if you were doing research on Abraham Lincoln, a letter written by Abraham Lincoln would be a primary source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: An account in a book of the contents of that letter written by Abraham Lincoln would be a secondary source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An account that was not quoting in full the document, yes, would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And historical research where you utilise primary sources is academically favoured, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure it is any more. There's always been a value attached to primary sources in the historical profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Certainly secondary sources should not be utilised when primary sources are available and could be utilised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not agree, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think secondary sources act as an important filter, echo of primary sources, and themselves become of great interest in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In this case, Dr. Donia, you were asked by the Prosecutor to write a report, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And to write a report with regard to the activities of a certain group of people at a certain time and place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The request was broader than that. I was asked to write a report on the broad historical background and context in which these alleged events took place, including the activities of groups relevant to the processes going on at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You heard -- I believe Ms. Korner indicated that you were watching on the monitor when Mr. Inayat testified about the searches and seizures that had been done in Prijedor and Banja Luka. Are we correct about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw part of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're aware that -- that those searches and seizures were done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And Mr. Inayat talked about going to places like the municipal building in Prijedor and Banja Luka and gathering official documents from those places. Those would be the kinds of records that an historian might be interested in looking at who is doing research into what was happening during that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would be one small group of types of records that would be of interest to the historian.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to know if in the process of preparing your report in this case that you were given access by the Prosecutor to all of those documents that were seized from Prijedor and Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: As you told the Trial Chamber on the first day of your testimony, you basically were relying on a group of documents which would be the group of documents that are contained in the two volumes we've been referring to for the last several days; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a little broader than that. There were additional documents that are not included here within the collection that I looked at, which included, as I indicated, the records of the Assembly of the Serbian republic and the ARK Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But in any event, it was a collection of documents that was chosen by the Prosecutor and not by you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think what you told the Chamber was: "Mr. President, I'd like to disclose that the Office of the Prosecutor invited me to review a limited set of documents on which some of these conclusions are based, and those documents consisted of the minutes and conclusions of the ZOBK and the Krajina and also the transcripts of minutes of the Bosnian Serb Assembly and some related documents to these."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You continued that: "In addition, I've looked at a great deal of periodical press and other documentation. I would just like to state that for the record." Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what you were really telling the Trial Chamber there was that your opinion was only as valid as the integrity of the selection of documents that was given to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that's not what I was -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My question was poorly worded. As the -- not just the integrity but the completeness of the series of documents that were given to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was not my message to the Chamber, no. The substantial bulk of information that I used in preparing this report in fact came from a much broader search of the periodical press of the time, some other documents that have been published subsequent to them -- to those times, memoirs, secondary accounts. The documentary base that -- the limited documentary base that I was asked to review, I reviewed in the context of all that information that I've gathered probably over the past several years.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I take it, then, that you have spent a great deal of time in the ARK region, in Banja Luka, Prijedor, places like that, actually doing original historical research.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I have never worked in the -- any of the regional archives of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the course of the work that you were doing for the Prosecutor in this case - and I think you've already answered that, but I want to make it clear that you have - did you receive from or send any correspondence to the Office of the Prosecutor regarding your work in this matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever request orally that the OTP supply you with any additional documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I've asked for copies from the Official Gazettes of both Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: As part of this particular project?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And did you receive those copies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Any --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they were available. I think a couple of them were not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. available, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Any other documents that you requested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever see any minutes of meetings of the Crisis Staff of ARK?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There may be one or two documents in this binder, but I -- I don't recall specifically. If -- if there is, I saw that. Beyond that, I have not seen minutes of crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to the ZOBK ARK Assembly, I believe you were provided with the minutes of the second, sixth, seventh, ninth, eleventh, fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighteenth sessions of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That sounds right. I believe that's the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I mean, if you want to go through and check what I did last night to try to make this accurate, you're free to. Do you want to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I take your submission that those were the ones that I reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My question, then, is: Have you seen the minutes of the first, third, fourth, fifth, eighth, tenth, twelfth, thirteenth, sixteenth, and seventeenth sessions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ask for them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I asked at one point if any other minutes of the assembly were in the possession of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I assume you got an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was told that they did not have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It would have been useful, I suppose, in trying to paint a complete picture of what was going on during this time to have been able to consult those.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I mean, that's why you would have asked for them; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I guess you'd have to agree that it's entirely possible that had you been able to see these other minutes, that that could have modified the conclusions which you arrived at and detailed to the Chamber yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's possible. Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to in the course of the rest of my examination, Dr. Donia, refer to some pages from a book. It's called "The War in Bosnia-Herzegovina: Ethnic Conflict and International Intervention," by Steven Burg and Paul Shoup. And I know that you're familiar with this book.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I know that you regard it as an authoritative source regarding the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it an authoritative source. I'd call it an important book that uses substantially the available documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree with the proposition that it is a work by two well-distinguished American scholars with a very impressive work, especially in regard to the issues in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I want to go very briefly through some history that you touched upon, and I'm going to go through it a lot more briefly than you did. You talked about the history of the Krajina areas, both in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Croatia, that borderland, the borderlands. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I believe what you explained to the Trial Chamber was that those borderlands through there have been for a very long time a kind of dividing line between what, for maybe simplified purposes, we might describe as a Christian west and a Muslim east, at least when the Ottoman Empire was in charge of everything there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that's an oversimplification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it is too.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The fact -- I would, rather, say it was a boundary zone between the Ottoman and Austrian Empires for the period from, say, the seventeenth century until the latter part of the nineteenth century.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And both -- both of those parties had made efforts to protect that border by stationing fighters, for lack of a better word, along that border?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I would only propose to modify that proposition by calling it a border zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because it was, in fact, a very extensive territory rather than a line, a piece of barbed wire that separated the two areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The point I'm trying to make is that people were sent there for the purpose of protecting that border zone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: As warriors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were recruited for that purpose, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And trained as warriors for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of them weren't trained, but they were recruited and moved there as whole families or extended families.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in some places that population group was Serbian Orthodox, and in some places that population group was Muslim.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the descendants of those people tend to have been living in that area in 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In -- in general, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can we go now just briefly again to the events in the Krajina area during World War II. It's probably the case, is it not, that well over a hundred thousand Serbs were slaughtered in that region by forces, primarily Croatian, that had aligned themselves with Nazi Germany?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The number is not certain. I would accept the hundred thousand number as an approximate number based on the sources that have -- studies that have been made of that since then. It may be high based on those demographic sources, but it's close.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: As many as 17 per cent of the Serbian population of Bosnia and Herzegovina were casualties of World War II. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. This slaughter was without regard to whether it was men, women, or children. They were just slaughtering people; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first Ustasha assaults on these communities, absolutely that was the case. Subsequently there was, of course, a lot of armed conflict, particularly between the Germans and Serbs in Krajina, which there was a less of a -- let's say there was some discrimination in which the warriors were principally males of military age.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And as you told us yesterday, the -- the atrocities, the slaughter, was especially pronounced in the Prijedor region and that explains the large monument that sits at Mount Kozara.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first part of your question is yes. The large monument is a monument to the partisan heroes who resisted particularly the German offensives and established a substantial territory that was outside of German control, particularly in 1942 and 1943.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And just a very short distance across the border in Croatia was the infamous Jasenovac concentration camp; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it would be virtually impossible to grow up in the Bosnian Krajina without knowing about that camp and the things that happened there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was, was it not, an extermination camp such like Auschwitz, Birkenau, and such places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you recall when Franjo Tudjman came to power in Croatia that he contended publicly that the numbers of people exterminated at Jasenovac was exaggerated and that the number of Serbs killed during World War II was exaggerated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His position on that was long before he came to power.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But, yes, that was his position advanced, as I say, already in the 1970s.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But it was widely circulated at the time he came to power.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was widely circulated well before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Also during World War II, there was a special SS unit established composed of Bosnian Muslims, was there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, when we get then to 1990, we are not really very far in terms of historical time from those events, are we?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Forty-five years at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Close enough so that there would have been a number of people alive in the Krajina who personally experienced some of the things you and I have been talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who may have lost a significant portion of their families.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And who might have had some particularly vivid memories of those times.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think you also know that it was -- it was such an astounding event - I guess is a way to put it - that it was certainly shared by those people, who experienced it with their children and their grandchildren.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And much was written about it, and it was part of curricula in schools.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, with a somewhat different approach in the socialist period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This theme was, of course, that atrocities were committed by foreign invaders and resistance to that was led by the partisans.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When we get to the events that really form the background of -- of the things that we're talking about in this case, that is, the dissolution of Yugoslavia, the creation of nationalist base parties, things occurred that -- that tended to bring those memories back to the fore. For instance -- let me be specific, and then you'll know what I'm talking about. I think it's the case that during World War II, the Croatian Ustasha symbol was a red-and-white chequer-board and that when the Croatian nationalist parties were created, that that chequer-board reappeared as a symbol. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that would be the kind of thing that would tend to be seen by victims of the prior Ustasha as something rather threatening and frightening, would it not? Provocative?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Many viewed it as provocative, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It certainly would have had some effect upon the mind-set of Serb people living in that Krajina area right next to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's -- I would have to assume about that, and I can't really speculate. But the restitution, if you will, of all these symbolic emblems by the national parties had that intent of reviving those recollections.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In that context, it would not be difficult to understand why people might want to arm themselves for protection, if for no other reason.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't share that conclusion, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You and I both live in the United States, and in fact you and I both lived for a time at the same time and place, in Houston, Texas. I think you would agree that it's not unusual in times of, say, a crime spree or something like that in the United States that people maybe without justification, but out of fear, will go to the gun stores and start buying guns. That happens, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That happens a great deal in Texas, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it happens other places. You know, you remember the Watts riots? The Watts riots was a big boon for the gun-making companies, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. You talked about the partisans in connection with the monument at Mount Kozara. The partisans, of course, turned out to be victorious at the end of World War II, to the point where the leader of the partisans, Tito, was able to establish a government which actually was a communist state, comprising all those components of Yugoslavia that existed until the break-up in 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And almost surprisingly, that government very effectively suppressed ethnic divisions immediately after some of the horrific events in World War II that we've been talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't quite formulate the achievements of the government that way. I think they so much emphasised the unity of the working class and permitted some modest degree of cultural expression by various nationalities that these ethnic tensions were reduced through most of the socialist period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, it wasn't just a thing that happened. It was a thing that was rather ruthlessly done by the Tito government to suppress public manifestations of ethnic intolerance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Public manifestations of ethnic intolerance were dealt with as criminal acts, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Rather ruthlessly at times.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At times. Particularly at the beginning of the Tito period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Some of the more vocal nationalists were -- I think "silenced" would be an appropriate word. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Silenced, imprisoned, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Power sharing between the nationalities was mandated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that that was actually the way it was done. There was -- power was exercised by the Communist Party, and that was to replace any nationally-oriented sources of authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you're familiar with what was called the kljuc, are you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what was the kljuc, the key?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The key was a system of appointments to various governmental social economic institutions, in which the various national groups were to be proportionally represented.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that happened in -- in the government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember the year that it was initiated, but a -- some form of, I'd say, national participation or participation from members of each nationality was encouraged from the beginning and mandated, I believe, somewhat later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that went across the board. It happened with regard -- it was with regard to government agencies, with regard to industrial concerns which were -- it's a socialist state, so they were government-owned and controlled -- with regard to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In principle, it applied universally. In reality, there were many institutions which did not conform to that guideline. And the JNA was a good example of one of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, by the time we get to 1989/1990, I think it is a fair statement that the officer corps of the JNA was weighted fairly heavily Serbian but it also had significant numbers of Muslim and Croatian officers also; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The -- "Brotherhood in Unity" was what -- a phrase that described what it was that Tito had established and tried to maintain in Yugoslavia after that -- the events of World War II; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The "Brotherhood in Unity" slogan dated from the beginning of World War II, was the partisan slogan really from the first days of its resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And actually, Yugoslavia prospered for many years under that kind of a system. The economy became somewhat robust, it became Europeanised in many ways. Yugoslavians were free to travel around the world on their passports. Tourism was big in various parts of Yugoslavia. It was a successful economic entity up until we begin to approach the break-up; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There -- there was a period of great economic success in the 1950s, and the economic problems really started to develop in the 1960s, and that in part explains the open borders and the willingness to allow Yugoslavs to work abroad and repatriate hard currencies. And the economic situation ebbed and flowed but was certainly a substantial crisis already by the late -- late 1970s.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. This is kind of a -- something I'm just curious about. Have you considered at all what effect on the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the beginning of the disintegration of Yugoslavia, what effect the war that the Soviet Union had been involved in Afghanistan had on that situation? Have you considered that at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly considered it in the context of the broader ills that beset the Soviet Union at that time and the impact that that had on Soviet reluctance to become engaged directly in the Yugoslav situation. I would say that would be the principal impact of that conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you if there might not also be the following impact: The -- what we now know as the Taliban - the other word you hear a lot is Mujahedin - those anti-Soviet Muslim fighters were seen in the Islamic world as having defeated one of the two greatest military powers in the world, that being the Soviet Union; true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't believe there's a continuity between the Taliban and the forces that were -- that defeated the Soviet Union, but in any case, the, let's say, support for fundamental Islam in a broad sense was certainly enhanced by the victory in Afghanistan of the defeat of the Soviets.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you also know, do you not, that some of those Mujahedin fighters that had been trained and fought in Afghanistan wound up in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1992, I believe. I don't know of 1991, but certainly in 1992, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if there was a perception that this was a group of fighters who were especially vicious, especially skilled, it is something that could have created a climate of fear about their arrival to fight against a group of people who were nowhere near as militarily sophisticated as the Soviet Union?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a speculation with a number of presuppositions that I can't really reach that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At least there are possibilities that that had an effect. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. I now want to go closer to time. The disintegration of Yugoslavia is something that has been written about by I don't know how many authors, many, many, many, and there is not universal agreement about the causes of why Yugoslavia disintegrated and broke up. I think our purpose here is not so much trying to understand why it happened but the causes, the result, the fallout from that disintegration. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It happened during a time when essentially there was a break-up of the Soviet Union and communist systems throughout Eastern Europe. The Communist Party was losing its dominance everywhere and the Cold War was ending; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the Communist Party in Yugoslavia came apart just like others did in Eastern Europe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A little bit differently. The Communist Party or League of Communists of Yugoslavia basically broke into its republican components in January of 1990, although that process had begun well before that, and had an afterlife of reformed communist parties in the various republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this -- this League of Communists was the party and the force which had enforced this kljuc or this key concept up until that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You touched very briefly on events I think maybe beginning, and I don't know but I think you do, beginning, I think, in the 1960s, where the Muslim people of Yugoslavia wanted to achieve the status of nationhood in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Bosnian Muslims --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- sought to be recognised as a nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Chamber what that means, to be recognised as a nation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, perhaps the way to explain it is to note that in Yugoslav partisan thinking, there were levels of recognition of groups, and the highest level was for a group to be recognised as a nation. So the nations that were recognised at the first partisan meeting in 1942 were Serbs, Croats, Montenegrins, Macedonians, and Slovenes, and they were defined as constituent stations within the Yugoslav Federation. The Bosnian Muslims aspired to receive that level of recognition, which would mean that they would be granted rights to be counted in the census, to have certain other group rights that were bestowed upon constituent nations as opposed to those considered of a minority or other peoples living in the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've talked about the kljuc or the key. It would have affected, would it not, the way they were treated under that system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That process of striving for nationhood by the Bosnian Muslims didn't happen without some expressions of nationalism which broke out, I suppose, in the early 1980s; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you ask the question again? I --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I may have asked it poorly, and I probably did. This struggle for nationhood on the part of the Bosnian Muslims contain within it a component of what was termed at the time sort of an extreme nationalism, Islamic fundamentalism, did it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It incorporated the -- the movement that actually dated to the months right after World War II known as the Young Muslims, and that group became one stream within the Bosnian Muslim political community that was considered by the government of Yugoslavia and others to be a conservative Islamic or fundamentalist Islamic group, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that group was suppressed by the government, including the arrest and trial of Alija Izetbegovic, and conviction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They did it after World War II and did it again in 1983.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You talked in your testimony about the appearance of the nationalist political parties, the SDA, the SDS, the HDZ. This was not the first time in Yugoslav history that there had been nationalist-based political parties, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There was a -- between World War I and World War II, there was a Bosnian Muslim political party, for instance, called the JMO, was there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: As the League of Communists began to fall apart and there was -- it became clear that other political parties would take its place, that there would be other political parties, competing political parties, in Bosnia --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a whole new area, and maybe this would be a good time to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think we'll pause for the moment. We will resume at ten to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, as we broke, we were beginning to discuss the advent of a multiparty system. Primarily, I'm concentrating now on Bosnia-Herzegovina. Okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Apparently, there was sufficient concern regarding what might happen if these parties were nationalist based, that -- as you know, the Bosnian parliament adopted an electoral law in March of 1990 that actually banned the formation of nationalist parties, did it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It authorised the formation of parties but excluded parties based on nationality or religion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that must have been based upon -- on an understanding that that could create some fairly significant, profound problems.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Also that same month a nationalist party, the SDA, was formed under the leadership of Alija Izetbegovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it's February on both dates, if I'm not mistaken. The constitutional amendments and the first -- not the formation of the party, but the formation of a -- an organising committee for the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. This law which had prohibited the creation of nationalist-based parties was declared unconstitutional by the constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina then, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And at the time that court -- the head of that court was a Dr. Kasim Trnka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And shortly after that, Dr. Trnka became an active member of the leadership of the SDA party, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If that is reported By Burg and Shoup in their book, would you contest it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what source they would cite, so I might.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. We might come back to that later in the day. And after that decision declaring the law banning nationalist parties was declared unconstitutional, then the SDS party was formed in July of 1990 and the HDZ party in August of 1990; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All three parties had a similar relationship to that law and to the constitutional court decision. They each formed organising committees prior to the constitutional court decision and engaged in certain party-like activities. But none of them formally held a founding assembly until after the June constitutional court decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the actual sequence in which parties were formed is, as I suggested, first the SDA, then the SDS, then the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I guess it depends on when the party was formed what that exactly means. I believe your order is correct for the actual constituent assemblies or founding assemblies of those three parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you have before you some excerpts from the book. Was that given to you yet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The registry has a copy for you, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, are you going to exhibit this extract from the book?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will leave that up to Your Honours. If you want me to make --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... ask the witness to refer to a document which maybe later on we will have to -- we might have to visit again, I would prefer to have it exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's make the document, then, Defendant's Exhibit number 1. I guess that would be DB1? Is that the way Your Honours want to do it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I would rather prefer the registrar to tell me exactly how she prefers, because this is more important for them than it is for the Court. Eventually we can follow. So I suppose that is how it's going to be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, DB1. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. DB1. The Prosecution has taken note of that? Thank you. Have you been given a copy -- a photocopy of the relevant pages from this book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have, Mr. President, but no footnotes -- none of the footnotes that are referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask the usher to give an actual copy of the book to Dr. Donia, because I think he may very well want to refer to the footnotes. And I apologise for not making those available to you, Dr. Donia. I should have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I noticed earlier that you had a copy of the book brought up to you. So that is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's right. We were handed the photocopies first thing this morning, so we got the book from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I saw it being brought up, so -- so you're happy. We don't have a copy of the book, but I think we can for the moment live with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We have another copy if it's necessary -- oh, we don't have another copy, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can move ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can follow in the book if you require spare copies, as long as we get it back for our file, because I have the book and the copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So please go ahead, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me refer you to page 46, which I think is the second actual page of text. I'll refer you to basically two -- two things there on page 46, going on over into page 47. I think the first thing you'll notice is the -- in the first -- second full paragraph: "The Constitutional Court, headed at the time by Dr. Kasim Trnka - who will later become an active member of the SDA leadership...." And that was the statement that we talked about a moment earlier. And then if you look at the last paragraph on 46, over into page 47, you will see that the authors say that: The SDA was established in March of 1990, the SDS in July of 1990, and MBO in October of 1990. My question, of course, is do you agree with the authors with regard to these matters which I have now brought to your attention? And please feel free to consult the footnote to see what the sources those authors used was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I respectfully disagree with the statement that the SDA was founded in 1990, or in March of 1990. I believe I've also in my paper cited a, frankly, better source for the constitutional amendments. If I can look a minute, I can find that for you. I note that footnote number 80, which regards the foundation of the SDA, is a footnote to an essay by Xavier Bougarel in a collection of essays and in no way could be considered a primary source. I am aware that Dr. Trnka at some point became a member of the SDA. I don't encounter him as an active member of the SDA leadership at any point early in the history of the party. I wouldn't necessarily contest this statement but would ask the question of what "later" means, because I think that it may have been substantially later that he became an active member of the leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: With -- I'm sorry. Are you finished?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I just look for my reference on the February constitutional changes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Absolutely, but as you're doing that, you should understand that I'm really not interested in precision with regard to these dates as much as I'm interested in the sequence. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm very interested in the precision, because you can't have a sequence without precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's true. That's true.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And if you'll note my footnote number 90 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're talking about page 32 of Dr. Donia's report. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. And I believe on page 31 I provided the date of 21 February 1990 that the Assembly passed a law. This is the last sentence on that page, that "... permitted political parties to organise but forbade parties based on national or religion," with a citation to Sluzbeni List, which is the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Maybe I will try to help both of you. It appears from your report, Dr. Donia, page 34 -- sorry, page 35, page 35, that the HDZ party held its founding Assembly in the Great Hall of Skenderija sports complex on my birthday, 18 August 1990. So that seems to be one affirmation that you are making.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The second affirmation that you are making is further down in the next full paragraph, at the very end of it. "The SDA held its Founding Assembly on the 26th of May in Sarajevo, attended by delegates from 73 ..." whatever.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that covers the second one. So certainly the SDA seems to have been founded, constituted before the HDZ for sure, according to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just to be precise about the formulation, Mr. President, it was the constituent assembly of those parties that were held on these dates, and using that criterion, yes, the SDA was founded first, the SDS second, and the HDZ third.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can we move --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The SDS on page 36, first paragraph, around the fourth line: "Around 3.000 Serbs attended the founding Assembly on 12 July 1990." This is, I suppose, the SDS. No?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does that coincide with what has been suggested to you by Mr. Ackerman? I mean, I don't want to take over. Please, Mr. Ackerman, go ahead. I was just trying to help clear the picture for you to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're doing just fine, Your Honour. Go ahead if you'd like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think the question that I asked you, Dr. Donia, was the SDA was formed in March 1990, SDS in July, and HDZ in August. Your report indicates that the SDS [sic] was not really formed until May but agrees with the July and August dates for SDS and HDZ. Fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. The formation of the parties, of course, was founded by elections, and in those elections most of the seats in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina were won by representatives of the three nationalist parties; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, there's one thing that I am really curious about, and please understand that I'm -- I don't understand it, and so I'm really asking for an explanation. If you'll look at page 51 of what we've now designated Defendant Brdjanin Exhibit number 1, down toward the bottom of the page where there's a little "x" and some brackets. They say that Fikret Abdic got the most votes and should have been the president as opposed to Alija Izetbegovic. I frankly don't know why that would be true, and is it true that that's what should have happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree kind of as a matter of principle that's what should have happened and indeed history might be different if it had, but the way that the inter-party agreement worked was that the party that won the most votes in the election was entitled to designate the president of the Presidency. The party that won the next most votes was entitled to designate the president of the Assembly. And the party that won the third-most votes was entitled to designate the president of the cabinet, essentially the prime ministership. That worked because the members of the Presidency selected the president and the members of the Assembly selected the Assembly president. So the party agreement among the three national parties was what led to this result.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you say "history might have been different if it had gone the other way," I take it you're referring to the difference in positions regarding what should happen in Bosnia-Herzegovina between Izetbegovic and Fikret Abdic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there are many differences between the two of them, and I'm not sure that -- I can't speculate on whether things would have been better or worse in the final analysis. But they were very different people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's true, is it not, that Abdic was in favour of trying to keep Yugoslavia together as a -- the entity that it existed as much as possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He was -- he was from that area up around Bihac, a significant Muslim stronghold up in that little pocket up in the corner up there. And he actually wound up fighting against the Bosnian army at one point with his group of Muslim fighters, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you look now, please, at page 63 of Defendant Brdjanin Exhibit 1. Down at the first full paragraph above the bottom, there's a sentence that begins "In the paralysis ..." Do you find that sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's the -- I'm sorry. I see the "nationalist revolution," and under that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: See the paragraph that starts with "Outside Sarajevo"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Go up six lines from there, and you'll see a sense starting "In the paralysis ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "In the paralysis that resulted and thanks to the attrition of non-Muslim cadres in the ministries, the government of Sarajevo came to be largely under SDA control. Since Bosnia-Herzegovina was a highly centralised state, the danger was real that the SDA and the Muslim ethnic community would effectively shut out the other ethnic communities from power, at least at the level of the central government." My question is: Do you agree with that statement by Burg and Shoup?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't. If I may, sir, he pronounces it Shoup.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, he's probably not listening today and doesn't know that I'm mispronouncing his name. So please don't tell him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It happens to him often.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you just go down to the bottom of that page, there's a sentence that starts with the words "In Gorazde." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "In Gorazde the Muslim SDA began a process of" -- and unfortunately I haven't copied page 64, but the quote goes on to say "began a process of weeding out Serbs from responsible positions." And you've got the book, so if you want to check that, you can. It's at page 63 and goes over on to page 64.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And do you agree with that? Are you aware that that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't agree with it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you telling the Chamber that that did not happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether it happened or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not if the Konjic municipality in April of 1992 the Muslim leadership there created a War Presidency and removed all Serbs from power in the Konjic municipality? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, it's true, is it not, that initially as these problems started to develop with Croatia and Slovenia wanting to secede and become independent, initially the SDS was in favour of Bosnia-Herzegovina remaining within a federal Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And took that position even if Croatia and Slovenia were to depart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The SDS, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And would you agree that international law tends to favour keeping a country together than having a country go into dissolution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't make a judgement on international law. I don't feel I'm qualified to -- to answer that question. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The SDA, under Izetbegovic, indicated that they had no interest in remaining in a federal Yugoslavia if Croatia were to secede and gain its independence. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I'd have to know when such a statement was made and in what context, because as I indicated in the direct testimony and in the paper, the SDA was trying very hard to straddle these two positions --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- of the HDZ and SDS and can kind of be found on various sides of that issue or be somewhere between them at various times.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it was immediately prior to June of 1991, when Croatia and Slovenia actually seceded, that Mr. Izetbegovic said that if Croatia left, then he couldn't in good conscience stay within a federal Yugoslavia. And if you agree with that, fine; and if you don't, fine. Just tell me how you feel about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it would not surprise me to find that statement made at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. At what point did the European Community get involved actively in what was going on in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In late June of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And one of the things the EC did was form a commission known as the Badinter Commission; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think the mission of that commission - that's a cute combination of words - the mission of that commission was to study and make recommendations regarding independence and regarding states that were trying to secede at that point from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was to accept applications for recognition of independence from those republics of Yugoslavia that wished to so apply and to evaluate those applications in terms of certain criteria.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And at least at the time that commission was formed, the issue of what was happening and would happen in the former Yugoslavia was pretty much up in the air as to what -- how it was to be treated, until about the 29th of November of 1991, when that commission determined that Yugoslavia was a country that was in fact in dissolution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there was substantial momentum prior to the Badinter Commission's being convened in the direction of independence for Slovenia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What the EC finally was resolved to try to accomplish through that commission in other ways was an orderly and co-ordinated recognition process for -- once it was clear that dissolution was happening -- of entities that qualified for recognition.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, in the process of trying to do that in an orderly and co-ordinated way, Germany jumped the gun and unilaterally on 23 December recognised Croatia and Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: An act that was entirely opposed by the United States and Britain and even the United Nations; yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was opposed by those countries and bodies, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In January 1992, that Badinter Commission with regard to Bosnia-Herzegovina determined that efforts to have Bosnia-Herzegovina recognised as an independent state within its existing borders were contradicted by declarations of Bosnian Serbs in favour of continued membership in Yugoslavia; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you ask that one more time?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. The Badinter Commission, with regard to Bosnia-Herzegovina, was faced with the proposition that unlike Slovenia and Croatia, a significant portion of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina seemed to be opposed to independence, that being the Bosnian Serbs, and wanted to remain within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Badinter Commission's conclusion noted the meeting of the Bosnian Serb Assembly on -- I believe it was the 21st of December, and that that Assembly had taken acts which tended toward the formation of a separate Bosnian state, and in order to determine what the popular feeling was, required a referendum to be held.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But that was -- was it not based upon the understanding by the Badinter Commission that there was a strong component of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was opposing independence, that being the Serbs? Let's just -- let me refer you to page 96 of the document you have in front of you. If you look about halfway down through the first full paragraph, you'll find a sentence that starts with "In the case of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Badinter Commission noted ...."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "In the case of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Badinter Commission noted that the government's efforts to declare an independent state within the existing republic borders were contradicted by the declarations of Bosnian Serbs in favour of continued membership in a Yugoslav state. It therefore ruled that the will of the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina to constitute the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a sovereign and independent state cannot be held to have been fully established. It suggested a referendum of all citizens of the Serbian republic -- of all citizens of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a possible means by which the popular will might be determined."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's the way I stated it. They did not make a determination that the Bosnian Serbs favoured continued membership in Yugoslavia. They accepted and noted the declarations, in fact, of the Bosnian Serb Assembly tending toward the formation of a separate state and therefore ordered that the popular will be determined via a referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. The Badinter Commission would have at least had some notion at this time of the ethnic make-up of Bosnia-Herzegovina certainly; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And they would have certainly had an understanding that there were three primary nationalist parties involved, the SDA, the SDS, and the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And by pronouncing that -- that the government's efforts to declare independence were contradicted by declarations of Bosnian Serbs in favour of continued membership in the Yugoslav state, by making that pronouncement, they were in effect saying that "Unless you can get all three of your ethnic groups to agree, that independence probably doesn't make sense at this point."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be precise about the declarations of the Badinter Commission, they made no determination about the will of the Bosnian Serbs or -- nor in fact did they consult the views of the SDS. They only cited the conclusion of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, which left open the question of whether those representations were in fact representative of a large number of Serbs or others in Bosnia, and that was the basis for their requiring a referendum. I note here you have a secondary source that you're referring to. I believe I referred to the primary source, which was published in Yugoslav survey, in my paper, to the language -- precisely to the effect that I've just indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And I don't think we're in disagreement. The point I'm trying to make is this: The Badinter Commission would have understood that other than the Bosnian Serbs, it appeared that the other constituencies in Bosnia-Herzegovina were in favour of a declaration of independence but didn't have a full understanding of the position of the Bosnian Serbs in that regard and therefore thought there ought to be a referendum.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what logic the Badinter Commission went through to arrive at its conclusions. Its conclusions in no way reflected an a priori understanding of the popular will of Bosnias, of Muslims, of Serbs, or Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It would not have been unrealistic for Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina to interpret what that commission had said as requiring a consensus among the three nations of Bosnia-Herzegovina before they would recommend independence; true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I can't agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, then why would it have made any difference at all to the Badinter Commission what the Bosnian Serbs thought about independence? It seemed to be the point upon which they refused to recognise the possibility.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My reading of their decision was that they were asking for a referendum to determine the popular will.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They didn't do that in Slovenia and Croatia, did they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not require a referendum in the case of Slovenia or Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's because there was apparently no group contesting the proposition that there should be independence, no significant group contesting that proposition in Croatia or Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There certainly was such a group in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Of significant size?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. About 600.000 of the Serbs of Croatia were opposed to independence for Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any idea why there was not a referendum called there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A referenda had already been held, I believe, in both Croatia and Slovenia, organised by local authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is there any indication in what the Badinter Commission determined that all they were looking for was a simple majority or that they were looking for a consensus among the national groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't -- to my knowledge, they did not define what would constitute the passage of that referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
