utterances.text: A -- a commission that has as its mission to try to make recommendations regarding an orderly process, one would not think that that commission would want to make recommendations that -- that would create disorder, and it was clear, was it not, after the actual referendum had occurred that a significant portion of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that being the Serbs, were very much opposed to independence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And it's possible, is it not, that the Serbs of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the leadership of the SDS of Bosnia-Herzegovina, believed that if they simply maintained, if they simply maintained an opposition to independence, that it was possible the Badinter Commission would never recommend to the EC that Bosnia-Herzegovina be recognised as an independent state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I've kind of lost your question in that. If you could kindly ask it again, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will. I'll try to be clearer. You would concede, I take it, that one of the things that the leadership of the SDS could have concluded was that continued opposition by the Bosnian Serbs to the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina could prevent the Badinter Commission from recommending the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina as an independent state.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's conceivable, yes. It's possible that they might reach that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you -- are you aware of a meeting that took place in early November of 1991 - I think that's when it was - between Izetbegovic and Genscher of Germany, Han Dietrich Genscher of Germany?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have a specific recall of a reference to it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you look at page 97 and just -- I guess the question that I must ask you then is: Does this refresh your recollection of this incident at all? It's the paragraph beginning with -- the first full paragraph, "This was the situation ..." And you may want to go back and read that so you know what the "this" refers to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I've read the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think we must go back now and talk a little bit about the way the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia operated with the collective presidency. You know what I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no, I'm not clear what you're getting at.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I'll be more clear. After the death of Tito, he basically in anticipation of his death left instructions for how the government of Yugoslavia would operate after his death, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The way in which Yugoslavia would operate after his death was enshrined in or a part of the 1974 constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right. And that 1974 constitution set up a -- a collective -- I think it's called a collective presidency.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So that there were representatives there from each of the republics plus Kosovo, and what other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Vojvodina. Thank you. And -- so that there was a balance there in the collective presidency that would make it difficult for any one particular nation to rule over the others. And that was the intention of the 1974 constitution, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And when Izetbegovic sees that there is a danger that Slovenia and Croatia could be recognised without the issues of Bosnia-Herzegovina being dealt with in that SFRY collective presidency, two votes that might help protect his constituency would be gone - that would be Slovenia and Croatia - and that would be why he felt like that would put him in a precipitous situation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be one of many reasons that he would be concerned with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And it was not clear at the time that recognition even meant withdrawal from the collective presidency, so that would -- that would be one of several considerations that he would have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. It was enough of a concern, according to Burg and Shoup, that Izetbegovic, before his meeting with Genscher was briefed by the German ambassador in Belgrade to make sure Genscher understood what would happen with unilateral recognition of Croatia and Slovenia, that this would create serious problems. Burg and Shoup say right after footnote 153: "The incident remains a puzzle. Izetbegovic would certainly have warned against limiting recognition to Croatia and Slovenia, especially if Germany took this step without the agreement of the remaining members of the EC. We have it on the testimony of a participant in the November 22 meeting, Michael Libal of the German foreign office did not warn Genscher of the danger recognition would pose for Bosnia." I don't know if you agree with Burg and Shoup about the facts of that situation, but you can tell me whether you do or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this is, of course, a secondary account based on memoirs and apparently a possibly private communication from a member of the German foreign office. I certainly find credible that there was a meeting between Izetbegovic and Genscher, but much of this must be looked at as speculative conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I think one of the problems that we have in what we're trying to do here is that there is a great deal about those days that is still not completely fleshed out and understood. There's still a lot of questions, aren't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would absolutely agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And that's -- I actually received a call from Professor Shoup two years ago, telling me that they were planning to do a revised edition of this book and asking me who he might search out in Sarajevo to help find some additional information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And in that kind of a situation where there is so much that is mysterious and unknown, we just kind of do the best we can, don't we?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe we must, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go to January 25th, 1992. In the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was a debate going on that day regarding the adoption -- the proposed adoption of a referendum of a proposal on independence -- a referendum on independence. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the measure, the proposal, was very much opposed by the Serb members or many of the Serb members of the parliament.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And at that time, the president of the Assembly, as you have told us earlier, was a gentleman named Momcilo Krajisnik, a Serb; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And Krajisnik, after several hours of debate, adjourned the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he attempted to adjourn the Assembly is the account in, I believe, the source that you're looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Assembly then went back into session, after the Serb representatives all departed, with an SDA member then acting as president of the Assembly; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now -- and the result was that the measure in support of a referendum then passed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Just to be accurate, the following paragraph here in the Burg/Shoup book on page 105 indicates there was 17 hours of debate and what they assess to have been a groping for a compromise prior to that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. We're going to that. That's where we're going next. But if you want to anticipate me in answer, that's fine with me because that's what -- that's what I wanted anyhow. My next question was: This session was one of those long sessions, 17 hours' worth of debate; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And throughout that day, all kinds of efforts were being made in private meetings of leaders and that sort of thing to try to come up with some kind of a solution that would create what would amount to a cantonisation or regionalisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina prior to the referendum being held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Much of that discussion centred around the quest for cantonisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And around midnight -- this 17-hour thing went late. Around midnight, it appeared that there had been an agreement reached between the SDA and the SDS for a regionalisation or a cantonisation that would make it possible for the referendum to go forward with everyone participating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you'll find that -- well, I guess I don't have the -- you'll find it on page 106, but I don't think I have a copy of it. Things then deteriorated again when Alija Izetbegovic became concerned that there were conditions being placed on the referendum that he could not accept.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Serb members then of the parliament suggested that the referendum proposal should be sent to the Council for Equality Among the Nations, which was -- was a proposal that had not yet been approved. But the idea behind that was that there would be a body that would have the power to overrule anything that the government might do that did not take into account the needs and desires and protection of any minority nation, very similar to the kljuc concept of Yugoslavia. And do you agree that that was what that Council for Equality Among Nations was designed to accomplish?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That doesn't have much to do with a kljuc concept, but it was designed to provide each -- representatives of each nationality to review as a nationality laws that affected the interest of their nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was -- really was a continuation, was it not, of the Yugoslav concept of "Brotherhood in Unity", that we have nations here that need to get along with each other and to some extent we need to enforce that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And that didn't work either, and so, as we've discussed, Krajisnik adjourned the session and the Serbs all left.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. You talked then yesterday about -- we're going to move forward now to February of 1992. The EC was still involved in trying to solve the Bosnia-Herzegovina puzzle, and a mediator by the name of Jose Cutilheiro took over the effort to try to find a solution; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Those efforts, in fact, had been ongoing from late 1991. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. On February 22 and 23, I believe it was, in Lisbon, there was a proposal put forward by Cutilheiro that involved the creation of again kind of a cantonisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that proposal was agreed upon in Lisbon, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We referred to this agreement yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, we did. I want to -- if you go to the very back -- actually, it's not the very back. It's pages 111 and 113 of the materials that I've provided to you. You'll see a couple of maps. And these are maps that were created during this process that was going on with Cutilheiro regarding this cantonisation idea that was accepted by all three parties in February. And the two maps that I've included are the one that Cutilheiro himself proposed and the one that was apparently drawn and proposed by the SDA. Do you see the two maps? You have them, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any quarrel with these being maps that came from that process with Cutilheiro at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The second map is presented in the book as a map adapted from Politika, which is a Belgrade newspaper. So I would not be able to certainly vouch a priori for its authenticity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you're not able to say that that is an accurate representation of a map presented by the SDA during that conference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not able to say that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If it is -- let's just -- just for the purposes of asking you one more question, if it is, you note, do you not, that there is virtually no difference between that map and the Cutilheiro map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there are a number of significant differences, but the big picture, snapshot, looks very similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we look at the area that we're concerned with here, north-west Bosnia, both maps place Bihac and Prijedor in the Muslim districts and then that large area centred around Banja Luka within Serb districts; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. After there had been this agreement, and "agreement" perhaps is a little bit strong because it hadn't been completely formalised, but there was an agreement in principle between the three parties in Lisbon to the Cutilheiro cantonisation idea. Almost immediately upon returning to Sarajevo, Izetbegovic announced that he had changed his mind and denounced and withdrew from the agreement, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not quite the case. He dispatched a letter to Mr. Cutilheiro in which, as I indicated yesterday, citing the Banja Luka Assembly that the proclamation of a constitution of the Serbian republic would make further discussions of the plan pointless.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Which was almost a pretense since if the plan were adopted, that other issue wouldn't arise, would it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a pretense.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. All right. I want to go to a different issue now. You have before you the documents that you were referring to yesterday, and under tab 12 in volume 1 is the Prosecution Exhibit 15. Let me know when you've found that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. If you look at the last page of the English translation of that document, the final paragraph is a paragraph you brought to the Chamber's attention yesterday when you were testifying about this document, and that paragraph is -- if this document is a legitimate document, that paragraph refers to the arming of Serbian people, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All of the parties, the Serbs and the Muslims and the Croats, were involved in the process of arming themselves as we get into late 1991, early 1992, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you'll look now back at Burg and Shoup pages that I've given you, at page 74, the last full paragraph down through footnote 54, where they say this: "All the while, arms were pouring into Bosnia. The JNA began a transfer of arms to the Bosnian Serbs. The Croatian paramilitary group - the Croatian Defence Force - was actively arming its members in Herzegovina. The Bosnian Muslim Green Berets were organised in fall 1991. According to Izetbegovic, they numbered between 35,000 and 40,000 when the conflict began. The more inclusive Patriotic League was formed at the same time and, in February 1992, drew up a plan for the defence of Bosnia. According to Sefer Halilovic, the League numbered 120.000 members by spring 1992." The first thing I'd like you to do is tell the Chamber who is Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sefer Halilovic was, I believe, the first commander of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He also happens to be under indictment at this Tribunal at this time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any quarrel with the pronouncement made there by Burg and Shoup regarding the organisation of all three of these parties, militarily arming themselves and so forth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as I indicated in my paper, there's I think reliable evidence that the Patriotic League was organised earlier, starting in May 1991. My -- I would just note that Halilovic was a great proponent of the Patriotic League and that number may be high. It may be exaggerated. But other that that, I would accept the statements here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I want to go now to -- as they say occasionally, "And now for something entirely different." The documents that we were dealing with yesterday, one of the things that you see from looking at those documents and studying those documents is the development of significant tension between Radovan Karadzic and what I will call the Pale group, and Vojo Kupresanin, Radoslav Vukic, Radoslav Brdjanin or what I will call the Banja Luka group. There was a significant battle going on between them, was there not, over the issue of -- of what kind of form the Serbs would resolve themselves into and where the seat of that government, whatever it became, was going to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. A substantial disagreement over the organisational form of Bosnian Serb organisations and also the seat of -- of its government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One of the -- one of the announced justifications for the formation of ZOBK and then ARK was that there was a contention by persons in the Krajina area that the concentration of economic resources in Sarajevo was causing the area to be economically neglected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think you indicated during your testimony that there really is not a great deal of -- of support for that proposition, as to whether that was an actual thing or simply a perceived thing; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If it was -- frequently -- frequently in life our perceptions differ from reality. It really doesn't make a great deal of difference, does it, whether that was the perception that that was happening or the reality that was happening that caused people to believe that it was important to do something to improve the economic situation of the Krajina by forming a regional organisation of some form?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I think it makes a great deal of difference whether a perception has some empirical basis or it does not. So I would not agree with your proposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You referred to statements made by Dr. Jaksic. Would you tell the Chamber who he is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dr. Jaksic was the director of the Institute of Economics in Banja Luka, and his party -- he was a member of the SDP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know that Dr. Jaksic was one of the forces behind the concept Bosnia-Herzegovina-wide of establishing regions for economic regions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Have you read his book about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I haven't either, because it's only in -- written in Serbo-Croat. It is not your contention, is it, that this whole concept of regionalisation was something that was invented by and emanated from the main board of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In fact, when the constitution of Republika Srpska, or the Serbian Republic of the BH, was drafted, it didn't even recognise the existence of ARK or other regional associations in its original form, did it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The constitution of Bosnian -- I'm sorry, which constitution would you be referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Serbian constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that original draft constitution that there was such a fight over regarding regionalisation and the capital.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what was in the -- what might have been in early drafts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We were looking -- and it would be hard for me to find it, but I probably can -- we were looking at some minutes yesterday where the whole meeting basically was an argument about the draft of the constitution. They were looking at failing to recognise the existence of regions and establish the existence of regions. Do you know what I'm talking about now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And my recollection is that the draft constitution as submitted on the 28th of February did recognise regions but didn't use the language that the Banja Luka group favoured, terms like "autonomy" and "sovereignty." That's my recollection of the difference between the draft constitution and the position taken by the ARK Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And the -- if you look at your report, at the top of page 66. The failure of those Pale -- the Pale crowd to do what the Banja Luka crowd wanted done resulted in threats to create a totally independent republic of the Krajina; correct? I think that's what you say there on page 66.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This meeting is in anticipation or on the eve of the proclamation of the republic -- the Serbian Republic on the 9th of January. And so in some sense, in anticipation of that meeting, they expressed this demand for that status for their entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And also the opposition to the capital being in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If I may, the Pale name is a bit premature because it wasn't until April that this central leadership of the SDS actually went to Pale. It was the Sarajevo group at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. The Sarajevo group, about to be the Pale group.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Brdjanin was -- expressed his views against the capital being in Sarajevo and said there would be no way to prevent the same old situation. And the same old situation he was talking about was what was perceived to be the economic neglect of the Krajina region; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And all of this agitation from the Krajina area was a direct challenge to the authority of Karadzic by the people from the region of the ARK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this was all going on at the same time that Karadzic was negotiating in the Cutilheiro context for a solution, which would have involved the cantonisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And we talked a little bit ago as all of this agitation coming out of the ARK as -- as being a basis that Izetbegovic used to abandon the agreement that had been reached in Lisbon in February.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His letters only cites the fact that a Serbian -- a constitution is about to be adopted by the Serbian Assembly, as reflected in the debates held in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right. And that -- then this -- this then prompted Cutilheiro to make the phone call you talked about yesterday, which in effect he told Karadzic he had to keep his Serbs in line if he was going to keep this thing together.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And as Karadzic made efforts to control the Serbs from the ARK region, the rift became wider, rather than narrower.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I think that the -- from this point in time, which is the 24th or 25th of February, the rift was resolved, not perhaps definitively, but the essential solution was reached within three, four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if you'll look at your report on page 67. After Karadzic returned from his phone call from Cutilheiro, the meeting degenerated into some fairly serious name calling, with Karadzic accusing Brdjanin of being out of step, of having no right to sabotage what they were trying to do. I mean, that's -- that's language that is not designed to repair a rift but I think make it wider, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was emphatic in his language in this Assembly, and there is more such language on the -- in the deputy's club meeting of the 28th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: However, the rift was essentially repaired at the time the constitution was adopted on the 28th and then endorsed by the ARK Assembly on the 29th in accord with the recommendation of Mr. Krajisnik that the leadership of the Sarajevo SDS meet with the ARK Assembly on the 29th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to refer now to Prosecution Exhibit 33. Now, this document is the meeting of the Assembly of 25 February 1992, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. Let's see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's under Tab 29A in my book. But that may not have any relation to yours at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I have the shorthand notes of the eighth session of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you look at page 44.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And on page 44, it's Karadzic that's speaking. And he says, does he not, that "We cannot allow that five people with personal ambitions destroy our chances. We are very close to achieving our strategic objectives. I do not object if someone has a better plan, Brdjo, for instance, who is responsible to this Assembly, and so he must be because he is a member of this Assembly. If he has a better plan, let him come out with it here." And then skipping just a little bit: "We do not see that he has a better plan." If you go then to the next document, Prosecution's Exhibit 34. And this document is a meeting of the deputy's club of 28 February 1992, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On page 36, Karadzic speaking again, down near the bottom of the page, the paragraph beginning "We can and we must renounce everyone who refuses to work the way we have agreed, Brdjo and all the rest. When Brdjo appears somewhere, he's like a bomb. He blows up everything. I won't allow it as a psychiatrist and as a party leader. He's crazy. He's not normal." Dr. Karadzic continues: "He doesn't know what he can do and what he can't do." Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's go now to Prosecution Exhibit 35. It's now 29 February 1992, in the Great Hall of the Banja Luka cultural centre. It's a meeting of the 14th session of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, and Radovan Karadzic and Momcilo Krajisnik and Nikola Koljevic and Velibor Ostojic from the Sarajevo Pale group are in attendance; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And Karadzic says, looking at page 2, and referring to efforts to have the Krajina region declared a republic: "If a republic of Krajina were declared, all Serbs outside this territory would suffer from the consequences of this decision." That was Cizmovic who said that. Karadzic then stressed that: "It would be a crime again the Krajina if it were declared a republic. Those who advocate such childish ideas are exposing the Serbian people to trouble." Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So he then characterises ideas proposed by Brdjanin as being childish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So on more than one occasion, it's fair to say, is it not, that Karadzic has publicly critical and in fact used language that could be characterised as humiliating with regard to Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In this time between the episode of his being interrupted in the council and this meeting, there are a number of instances of such language in the deliberative bodies with Karadzic so referring to Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ackerman, I think if you can conclude on this part, if that doesn't take you more than a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm in a very good spot to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will resume at ten to one, ten to one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're waiting for Dr. Donia, may I ask what time Your Honour's going to be sitting today? Simply there are a couple of short administrative matters that I want to raise with Your Honours before Your Honours rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long do you anticipate it will take you to finish your cross-examination, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm guessing that I have about an hour and a half left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That means we'll go into tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I expect -- I expect that I would go into tomorrow with what I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And how long do you anticipate these two administrative matters will take?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Five minutes, no more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I would suppose -- do you have any objection at all if we start with these two administrative matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, no problem at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So I will suppose you do that first. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's to do with the - I'll say that again - decision that Your Honours handed down the day before yesterday on the Rule 92. May I say genuinely, respectfully, very, very helpful to all of us because we see how Your Honour's mind works. All I wanted to say about that was in relation to Witness 7.167 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait. I haven't reached that stage as yet where I can memorise the witness numbers and the names. I have it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour said that he, because of some of the information that he gave, he should attend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, what I have to say is this: We have a large number of live witnesses already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That particular witness would have provided, had Your Honours allowed it, corroborative evidence to be given by two other witnesses. In those circumstances, we do not propose to call him, so that that's quite clear. I should say that this is not to be taken as something we will adopt in each and every case, so that the Defence feel by objecting to each Rule 92 witness that we will drop them. But here we do feel that it's unnecessary to call him because that evidence is effectively already covered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this is 7 -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's the first matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In fact there are three matters, really. The second matter is this: We are in the process of pre-numbering the exhibit bundles that have been tendered for Banja Luka municipality. We will provide the Defence with the index showing the pre-numbering. In addition to that, Mr. Inayat is at present carrying out on paper the same exercise that he carried out in court, in other words, individually identifying each document. That, we hope, will be provided to the Defence tomorrow morning. We would ask that if despite that information, there is still going to be an insistence that evidence is given before Your Honours may admit those documents, that we be notified and before we start the evidence from the first witness, and we will put Mr. Inayat back into the witness box. Your Honour, in any event, we intend to for this reason: There's a short - and I mean short; it runs to about 25 minutes - video, which we think may be helpful to Your Honours because it shows many of -- it's one that we made ourselves, but it shows many of the areas that this case will be coming. And I think it helps to look at the actual areas. Finally, Your Honour, can I just ask this: Because we're engaged in the process of planning ahead for this case, it would be helpful if Your Honours and the other branch of this Trial Chamber were able to give any information in the near future about when the Stakic case is likely to have a start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am not in a position to tell you that for the moment. Hopefully I should be in a position, but I can't anticipate any -- any day, anyway. But we will inform you. We will inform you. But we are not in a position to state anything for the present.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. Now, with regard to what Ms. Korner has suggested, not with regard to Stakic, not with regard to the video, but with regard to the planning ahead, is that acceptable to the Defence? Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And with regard to future motions based on 92 bis, I'll be very short but I'll make a recommendation. Just food for thought. And then perhaps when you have thought about it, as Milton would have put it, "inwardly digested it," then we can come back and discuss it. My suggestion to you is that provided at -- that at no time -- your right to cross-examine, in any case, the witnesses is maintained, very clear, and guaranteed to you -- in fact you have a right to that -- perhaps you could, barring few and far between incidents, adopt the procedure of accepting motions by the Prosecution for submission of evidence under 92 bis, because in actual fact, I mean, provided there is nothing illegal or which cannot be permitted under 92 bis in the text and the content of those applications, I suppose your rights remain completely unprejudiced. If cross-examination is forthcoming, not just guaranteed but -- I don't know. Think about it. I mean, the whole idea is to avoid unnecessary work for the Chamber so that we can move ahead. In other words, the same results would be achieved in any case, because there is always the right to cross-examine. So if we can agree, that will at least save on the time of the examination-in-chief and bring on the witnesses, if necessary, to have them cross-examined by you, and the whole scope of the exercise would have been achieved. I don't know. Think about it. There may be pros and cons. Perhaps we can discuss it further some other time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I understand Your Honour, and I think what you're saying is this: If the Rule 92 bis application is improper in that it is statutorily deficient --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is no question about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- then it should be raised. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Like you did, and correctly so and rightly so, in some instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But otherwise, if it is a situation where it is statutorily proper and yet someone who I wish to cross-examine, all I really need to do is let you know that that's someone I wish to cross-examine and not go through the rest of that procedure. I assume that's what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ackerman, you are assuming right. Basically what happens is in that in the majority of the cases, when you go through, you read through the statement of the witness that is being proposed to be presented in written form without producing the witness -- there are some borderline cases. There are some cases where it is very obvious. There are some cases where it is borderline, and there are some cases which simply do not exist but which are raised just the same for reasons that sometimes we do not understand. What I am suggesting is that unless, unless the objection that arises out of the Rule itself is really manifest on the face of the document itself, you let it go. We admit the statement. You make it clear that you want the witness here for cross-examination. We would have saved a lot of time on examination-in-chief and then we can concentrate on the cross-examination. I mean, it's a suggestion which -- something that we discussed, Judge Janu, Judge Taya, and myself, and we thought of putting it forward to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's a very good idea and I'm in complete agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you think about it and we'll see if it's practical or not. Of course you are not expected not to raise objections when they ought to be raised and when you are practical about raising them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I'm totally in agreement. I think it's a brilliant way to do it. It's a good idea. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Ms. Fauveau, I do not expect a definitive reply from you because obviously you have to refer the matter to your two colleagues, but I hope that even on your part you understand that this is -- what is being suggested is not to avoid work but to cut on unnecessary -- unnecessary waste of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I completely agree with you, and I'm sure that my colleagues shall also agree with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. That, I suppose, would be agreeable to the Prosecution as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may put a slight potential restriction on this. Some of the witnesses that we have selected to submit to Your Honour should be heard under Rule 92, which only requires attendance for cross-examination if Your Honours order it. There are good reasons; for example, age or infirmity. So I'd like it taken on a case-by-case basis if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't have to mention that or refer to that. Point taken, and that's how it will be, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the other thing I should have mentioned: In relation to the evidence or the transcript of the late Colonel Kranjc - I'm sure it's not pronounced "crunch," Kranjc - it seems to us a sensible place to deal with that matter will be after the last witness for the Banja Luka municipality who will be dealing with military aspects, and, therefore, Your Honours will be able to assess the weight or otherwise of that transcript after you've heard that evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And also, also in the meantime, maybe because, as I take it - if my memory is not failing me already - Mr. Ackerman has not objected now to the admission of -- of that testimony because it's -- we're talking about the testimony, evidence given in Tadic, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely. It doesn't affect his client at all. It only has an effect on the case against General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will -- actually, I think it is wise to wait to give a time, and we wait until maybe the counsel for General Talic would have had enough time to consider, reconsider their position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then obviously it is a point which would need some submissions, which has been decided by this Tribunal before and on which there have been some -- on which there has been some controversy. Anyway, I mean I do not want to open the chapter now. I agree with you. Perhaps counsel for General Talic should make a note of what Ms. Korner is suggesting, that this matter will come up for deliberation towards the end or at the very end of the Banja Luka chapter. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with Mrs. Korner, and I think at the end of this part it would be appropriate to decide on the admissibility of the transcript of Colonel Kranjc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think we can call Dr. Donia again once more. We will stop at -- as usual, at quarter to two, Mr. Ackerman. So you have 35 minutes. And if you feel more comfortable stopping earlier, you are closing a chapter or part or whatever, I mean you are at liberty to do that. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Donia, are you ready to go forward?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I said, "Now for something entirely different and in brief." Rather than go to the document -- I think you'll remember the document I'm talking about. It's Prosecutor's Exhibit 37, and it was that document which instructed from Vojo Kupresanin to municipalities that they had no obligation to assist in holding the referendum of the 29th of February. You remember the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All I wanted to ask you was: You have no information or document, do you, that any effort was made to actively prevent the referendum from going forward, to prevent it from happening in that same manner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Near the close of your testimony yesterday, you were talking about the superior armament of the JNA and as it became the army of Republika Srpska, and it occurred to me that the impression that may have been left that there was -- in fact, I think it was almost said that there was very little Muslim or Croat military capacity in the area that we're talking about. During -- also during your testimony, you mentioned that there was dispute - and when I say "dispute" I mean military dispute, that there was actual fighting - over the corridor that would connect the Krajina area to Serbia, and it's the corridor that I want focus on for just a moment. Do you agree that this corridor was actually seized and closed off by a combined Croatian-Muslim offensive early in the war, which offensive advanced on the city of Doboj and placed it under siege?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you look, please, at page 133 of the Burg and Shoup book, beginning with the paragraph "In June 1992 ..."? Do you see what I'm referring to? Page 133. It's the last -- it's the last page of defendant Brdjanin Exhibit 1. Have you found the paragraph I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It reads, does it not: "In June 1992, the Serbs launched their first attack in the war, most likely with the forces from Serbia, and won back areas seized by the combined Croat-Muslim force in Central Bosnia in May." That's what it says, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to quarrel with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just don't know if I can accept it at face value or disagree with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It goes on then after another sentence about Bihac: "The Serbs also failed to establish a secure corridor in the north between Banja Luka to the west and Semberija and Serbia to the east. They were unable to take the town of Gradacac, which lay to the south of the corridor, or the town of Orasje to the north." That's what Burg and Shoup say; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And again I take it it's your position that you just don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I see a single footnote here to I believe a story by Borba of the Belgrade newspaper, and it may be I just don't know. On that basis, I would not conclude that this would be a definitive account.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Look, please, then, if you will, at Prosecution Exhibit 33, page 60.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I have that in front of me, page 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. The speaker is Vojo Kupresanin. And if you look at the bottom of page 60, Mr. Kupresanin says: "I think we know what will happen if the Republic of Krajina is proclaimed. We don't hold Doboj. We do not have a crossing to Semberija. We cannot wage war for even five days because we will find ourselves without fuel." That tends to be confirmation, at least in part, of what Burg and Shoup are saying about the corridor and Doboj being in the hands of non-Serb forces, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It doesn't sound from this like the Muslim Croat forces who are able to keep the Serbs from catching the towns of Gradacac and Orasje and are able to take that corridor and hold it is a hollow force, incapable of any military activity, because of the superior armament of the Serb forces, does it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the -- there's two parts to your question, I think. One is concerning the Croat forces. And I would say as far as the Croat forces is concerned, your statement is correct. The Muslim forces were in worse shape than the Croats at this point and were -- were characterised by these local TO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But it's safe to say the Muslim forces were rapidly being supplied with significant weaponry, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends a little on the area and the particular location of units that you're talking about. And I just don't have information about how that process went forward at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you if you know this: Do you know that in the municipality of Konjac there was a major Yugoslavian arms manufacturing facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know also in the municipality of Konjac there was a major cache of weapons and materiel at a place called Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know that in April of 1992 Muslim forces took control of both that arms factory and the Celebici cache, if it existed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm aware that they did that. I wouldn't know that it was April, but I would believe that that's about the time that it took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. On Tuesday, you were discussing the decisions in the various municipalities to join the ZOBK. In your testimony, you indicated that Banja Luka did not vote to join until the end of April 1991, significantly after the others had voted to join. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I believe it was the 29th of April or within a day of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in connection with that testimony, you mentioned that one SDS member objected when Banja Luka voted to join ZOBK. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know who that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe I noted it in a paper, but I can't recall right offhand who that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were talking about the various municipalities in that region that were invited to join. Were there any municipalities that were part of the ARK region that were not invited to join?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I looked at the -- interpreted the invitation, it was an open invitation to all municipalities in the ARK area, including the areas of Cazin, Bihac, and Velika Kladysa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There's a reason I asked that. On page 48 of your report, you have a Table 2. You have a list of the nationality and municipalities invited to join ZOBK, apparently after the assembly; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what I'm wondering is were there municipalities that were not invited to join that were located in this ARK area that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe the invitation to join was an open one. But exactly who it may have been extended to and who it was not, I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you -- and maybe it was just with me that this impression was left. But I think the impression was left from your testimony that there was something extraordinary and bizarre, if looking at Table 2, about an invitation to municipalities which had virtually no -- no Serb members to join. And if every municipality in the ARK area was invited to join, that wouldn't really be very significant, would it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've been -- I think I spelled out my understanding of this invitation process at this point was that it was voluntary. It was extended to municipalities which had -- which did not have a Serb majority, as well as those that had a -- either a substantial Serbian population or a Serbian absolute majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to do a bit of skipping around. The -- and maybe we can do it rather quickly without having to look at all these documents. The Prosecutor's Exhibit number 25 is the Variant A/B document. And the Variant A/B document -- I do have to look at it. If you look at the document up in the upper -- and I'm looking only at the English translation, of course. On the first page, in the upper left-hand corner, it indicates that its source is the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia and Herzegovina Main Board; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you go, then, to its very last page, it indicates that the source is the SDS Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any indication that there was even such a thing on December 1991 as an SDS Crisis Staff, beyond this document itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were -- I don't know that this is a definitive source that I would accept. But reports of an SDS Crisis Staff being formed as early an October 1991, they were carried in press reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you've heard of it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- prior to December 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. This particular document we're referring to, this Variant A/B document, yesterday you characterised it as a complex document; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it's couched more in terms of recommendations to the various municipalities than it is orders that "you must do this," although there's some later material that you're probably going to want to talk about. But that's the way it's couched, in terms of its language, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You would disagree.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would suggest it's very clear that -- for example, in point one, the second item on page 2: "The tasks, measures, and other activities that are laid out in these instructions will be carried out in order to increase mobility and readiness."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I guess you'd agree with me that one of two things is true: It either was seen by certain people as simply being a series of recommendations or ideas; or certain people simply ignored it because it has a date of December, and in March there were still municipalities that had not followed it at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I would opt for the second explanation simply because there was so much resistance to these instructions expressed, starting on the 11th of December and, in fact, a number of municipalities after the instructions were issued. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So the SDS was not marching in -- toward this objection. There was quite a lot of dissension about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, yes. Dissension and even resistance in various municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, one thing that -- that I think maybe has not been made completely clear, and I think it's the case that in many of the municipalities where Serbs were in a minority, and therefore Variant B would have come into play, that the Serb municipalities that were formed were secretly formed, that they were not public but secret organisations. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, some of them were. Many were announced publicly at the time they were formed. There's one case where I think in the -- one of the Sarajevo suburbs they took the decision on the 3rd of January and announced it on the 10th of January publicly. So I think both cases were true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them were secret.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's really all I was asking. Could you look, please, at -- it's tab 40 of Prosecution Exhibit 44.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This is a communication, is it not, from Vojo Kupresanin of the Autonomous Region of Krajina to the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it is dated 17 July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know of any communication, either from the -- the ARK or its Crisis Staff to the Presidency of the Serbian republic, or any communication from the republic to ARK or its Crisis Staff between the dates of roughly the 1st of April, 1992, and this date 17 July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have to review this material, but I -- I don't know offhand of any.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Have you seen any response to this document by the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have anything that would make it possible for you to state with certainty that it was even sent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I note it's signed and stamped, but I think that's no guarantee that it was sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: These assemblies, and we've talked for the last several days about various assemblies, we've talked about the SDS assemblies, the assemblies of -- of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the assemblies of ZOBK and ARK, all of these assemblies are, by design, chambers of delegates, basically, in the form of a formally deliberate legislative body. That's kind of a basic view of them, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And legislative bodies basically function in democratic institutions as a group of elected representatives of the people whose task is to pass laws and resolutions and things of that nature, to govern the particular entity that they are an assembly of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the way they function in democratic institutions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And there is another -- as a general proposition, there are two additional bodies. There is an executive that carries out the laws that are passed by these assemblies or legislatures, and then usually there's a third branch which is the judiciary. Fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Not quite so clear-cut in some societies, but as a general principle, I would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you told us yesterday that the whole concept of a Crisis Staff was to be a body that would replace and take the place of the Assembly when under crisis conditions the Assembly could not meet and conduct its business.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think I characterised it as a body that would act in the name of the Assembly under certain specified conditions, war, threat of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think what you said, which probably doesn't -- isn't exactly correct, was that it was a body created to carry out executive functions in place of the Assembly, and the Assembly doesn't carry out executive functions, does it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it can. The formulation, as I understand it, the two organisations that existed were the Assembly per se and the Executive Committee, and the Executive Committee was not really an independent executive branch. It derived its authority and was kind of an executive organ for the -- for the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, looking specifically at the ARK Assembly, there was an Executive Committee of the ARK, was there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that Executive Committee was headed by a person by the name of Nikola Herceg; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was one of the two people who headed it, I believe, during the time that I looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And do you know or do you not that that Executive Committee continued to function on virtually a daily basis throughout the entire period from April to December?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From April to December of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1992. No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you go now please to Prosecution Exhibit 52.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yesterday you pointed out to the Trial Chamber language from page 2 where Karadzic is talking basically about how brilliant it was for him to ask for Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you aware of a time when Karadzic tried to fire Mladic, remove him as Commander of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not specifically. I know that relations were not great between them at several points in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you aware that there was a time when -- when the General Staff basically threatened to revolt if he insisted that Mladic be removed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm kind of going to somewhere else. Maybe this would be a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That brings today's sitting to an end. Dr. Donia, I'm afraid you will have to come again tomorrow, and hopefully Mr. Ackerman should finish his cross-examination of you within an hour. Is that correct? And then of course there is the further cross-examination from the Defence team for General Talic, which should not take long according to what Ms. Fauveau hinted yesterday. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in relation to cross-examination on behalf of General Talic, can I just mention this: It is General Talic's defence who have been making, if I can put it this way, not impolitely, the most song and dance about what they describe as the Prosecution's view of history. I have no doubt that Ms. Fauveau has it well in mind, but if there is a serious dispute on anything that Dr. Donia has said such that they intend to call an expert on it, it should be put to Dr. Donia, otherwise we'll end up having to have Dr. Donia back again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, Dr. Donia will certainly not come back again unless his presence and statement is required by the Trial Chamber itself. I mean, Dr. Donia's cross-examination will be concluded tomorrow and that will be the end of Dr. Donia. I'm quite aware, because more or less I suffer from almost a photographic memory, of what Mr. de Roux had said, that, "Mrs. Korner, you bring Dr. Donia. We are not impressed. We can bring as many Dr. Donias." So you are obviously entitled to bring as many Dr. Donias as you like, but you are expected to conclude the cross-examination of this Dr. Donia tomorrow, and that will be the end of the story of this Dr. Donia. Then obviously you're sure you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, A, there's re-examination. I know Mr. Cayley does have a few matters that he wants to deal with in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's tomorrow. Your Honour, the point I'm really making is that unless it is put to Dr. Donia what is in dispute, Your Honour won't be able to hear how he deals with it, whether he agrees with it or doesn't agree with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. The chapter will be closed tomorrow. I expect the cross-examination from Ms. Fauveau, because she's the one who is present. And that will conclude matters, as far as I am concerned, for General Talic, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, perhaps I think at the moment I'm not making myself quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, tomorrow's cross-examination is not going to be the introduction for a further cross-examination later on or for a further request to bring Mr. -- tomorrow Mr. Donia -- we conclude with Dr. Donia tomorrow, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because otherwise you can't hold the trial like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. What I'm saying is this: Effectively it goes back to the Rule I referred Your Honour to earlier, that is for the Defence to put its case. In other words, if they say Dr. Donia is completely wrong about an aspect, that must be put, because otherwise if they call an expert and it's never been put to Dr. Donia, so he hasn't been able to explain why he agrees or disagrees with that, the net result is that we may be having to make an application to bring him back. That's all I'm saying, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I would say that that request is almost preposterous. I haven't yet chosen an expert on history. I haven't had a chance to talk to my expert on history. I haven't prepared any testimony by my expert on history. And I am not an expert on history myself. And I have no idea what I might learn in talking with that expert that I want him to testify about when he comes here. So the proposition that I should tell Dr. Donia today what it is that expert is going to say, so he can either accept it or deny it, is just ridiculous. That just can't happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you are moving one step further than what Ms. Korner said. Ms. Korner --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what Ms. Korner has said, that if you are contesting something from what Dr. Donia said in his examination-in-chief or in his report that was filed by Prosecution, you do it now in the course of your cross-examination. You will -- the way that this Tribunal -- this Trial Chamber looks at things is that you knew beforehand that at some point in time in the course of the hearing of this trial, there would have come up the historical aspects. And I cannot allow a situation to obtain whereby someone comes and says, "But I did not prepare that part before we started the trial." No. You are expected to have prepared that part. And if you haven't, you will have to suffer the consequences. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I totally agree. That's not what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So in other words, I mean, to me it's difficult to reconcile what you are saying, especially that you agree with me, that what you are asserting, that you don't even know who your historical expert is going to be. You are expected by this Trial Chamber to have already known who your historical expert is going to be and to have consulted him before actually starting your cross-examination of Dr. Donia. That's how trials ought to be conducted. Otherwise, we would be swimming in a notion which -- ocean which is even vaster than all the oceans of the world put together, and we would never start and we would never end. Okay. So we'll rise. We'll reconvene tomorrow 9.00, this same courtroom again.
